Chapter 5: Everyday Words, Hidden Histories
Have you ever stopped to think about the words you use every day? Underneath the surface of our conversations, there’s this fascinating world of hidden stories—ones we rarely notice. Most of us never ask where our words come from, or how they’ve changed as the years have rolled by. But honestly, every sentence we speak is like its own little archaeological dig, filled with memories of past lives and faraway places.
Let’s start with something familiar—food. If you look at the words for animals in England—like "cow," "pig," and "sheep"—they’re mostly old English. But when it comes to the meat itself, words like "beef," "pork," and "mutton" come from French. What does that tell us? Well, it’s a story about who did the work, and who got to enjoy the meal. The farmers used those old words, while the nobles—sitting at the table—used the new ones. Over time, both sets of words stuck around, each carrying its own bit of history.
Now, think about the words we use for law and government. So many—like "court," "judge," and "parliament"—arrived with the Normans, along with their systems of power. Back then, French was the language of authority. But as the years passed, English slowly crept back in, changing the way people talked—and even thought—about justice and leadership.
Even our most ordinary words have surprising backstories. Take “window,” for example. It comes from the Norse “wind eye,” which paints a picture of a time when homes were just holes in the wall to let the breeze and light in. Or the word "sky," borrowed straight from the Vikings. And "egg"—it replaced an older English word that simply faded away.
It’s amazing how language is packed with these hidden tales. Someone might use a word they picked up in a distant port, never realizing its journey. Or maybe a child invents a new phrase, and somehow, within a generation, it becomes a regular part of what we all say. English is never finished. It’s always changing, always growing.
Most of the time, we take our words for granted. But every now and then, curiosity sneaks in. Maybe you catch yourself wondering why a phrase sounds a little odd, or why a word means what it does. And in those moments, the adventure of English really comes alive—not as some far-off history, but as a living, breathing part of your everyday life.
